Chapter 6: The Roots of Psychosis—When the World Becomes Too Much.
There are moments in life when the world just feels unbearably heavy, aren’t there? For some people, that weight presses down so hard, the boundary between themselves and the world starts to blur. The mind, searching for any kind of safety, might retreat into its own private reality. And you know what? That’s not a weakness, or some kind of failure. It’s actually a powerful sign of survival—the mind doing whatever it can to protect itself, even if that means stepping away from what others call “reality.”
Imagine a teenager, overwhelmed by nonstop chaos at home. Arguments echo through the walls, and every day feels like walking a tightrope. School doesn’t offer any relief—the pressure to fit in is relentless. One afternoon, she’s sitting alone in her room, and suddenly, the world outside feels far away. Her thoughts become strange and unfamiliar. She wonders, am I disappearing? Or is the world itself slipping away?
Most folks have no idea how thin that line can be—between just feeling overwhelmed and actually losing touch with reality. When the world feels unsafe, the mind’s defenses can really kick in. Some people withdraw into silence, some create elaborate fantasies, and others might even start hearing voices or seeing things that aren’t there. As frightening as these experiences can be, they’re not random. They’re the mind’s way of shielding itself from pain that just feels too much to bear.
If you really listen, you start to see that psychosis isn’t just a bunch of strange symptoms. It’s a response—a way of coping when the world becomes overwhelming. The person isn’t “crazy.” They’re just trying to survive in the only way that makes sense to them in that moment.
The real challenge isn’t to force someone back into a reality that feels hostile. It’s about helping them find safety, meaning, and connection again.
Therapists who truly understand this don’t rush to correct or confront. They show up with steady, calm presence. They offer a sense of safety, so the person can start exploring their experience without fear. And with patience, and trust, it’s possible to return to the world—not because all the pain is suddenly gone, but because now, it can be faced together.
